text: May Mobility; City of Gainesville 3.2 Updates to Selected Site Examples of Prototype AMDs Of the 10 early deployment sites tracked throughout NLR’s AMD research studies, several have matured to a level that represents early prototypes of the AMD network system concept in which AV technology provides essential circulation services within a geographically defined district. Although most of these AV fleet services are not running completely unattended (most have safety attendants or safety drivers), all encompass substantially advanced AV technology with most of the driving tasks performed with a high level of automation. In some of these sites, the AV fleets use an operating mode capable of on-demand service, with technologies that range from small- to medium-size transit vehicles. These sites include the following: • Site #2 in Arlington, Texas • Site #6 in Ann Arbor, Michigan, sponsored by Mcity, University of Michigan • Site #7 at the Rivium District near Rotterdam in the Netherlands (on-demand service is under development, with fixed-route service provided during most hours of operation). 14 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. These three prototypes of an AMD have been in continuous operation for multiple years, with continued improvement to the automation features and expansion of their coverage area. The status of selected sites is briefly described in subsections that follow. Other sites also in operation are using AV applications in fixed-route and fixed-schedule passenger service modes, such as: • Site #4 in Jacksonville’s Ultimate Urban Circulator (U2C) These sites are progressing through their progressive development phases, with their progress described in subsections that follow. More than half of the initial 10 sites have terminated operations as of the date of this third edition publication. One of these, Site #8 AV shuttle deployment in Denver at the Colorado School of Mines, is also discussed in a following subsection. This project’s documented findings provide an important reference for AMD implementation because of the insights gained on the challenges to achieving fully automated deployments. The issues that caused cessation of operation at Site #8 are significant challenges common to many of the early AV deployment sites as well as future AMD deployments. 3.2.1 Arlington RAPID Service RAPID is a form of on-demand AV fleet service embedded within Arlington’s citywide shared- ride microtransit service called Arlington On-Demand. As shown in Figure 7, this automated transit service operated from March 2021 to May 2025 within an area that surrounds the University of Texas at Arlington campus and downtown Arlington. RAPID service is designed to provide shared-ride service for multiple parties in real-time, on- demand dispatch operating mode. It is similar to what is also being called “robotaxis” but provides shared or pooled rides as opposed to single-party service. RAPID provides a direct ride from the passenger’s origin to their destination or with only a few stops for other shared-ride passengers along the special travel route.
